headline: 16mmol/L Blood Glucose Reading: Is It Accurate? Troubleshooting, False Reading Causes, and Safe Next Steps
description: Got a 16mmol/L blood glucose reading? 22% of home test results are false—learn how to verify if it’s accurate, spot false high causes, and take safe next steps for prediabetes, Type 1 or Type 2 diabetes.

mainEntity.name: Can a 16mmol/L blood sugar reading be a false positive?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, up to 22% of home glucose readings are inaccurate per 2023 Diabetes Care research. Common causes include expired test strips, dirty finger pads, uncalibrated meters, or high doses of vitamin C. Always verify the reading with follow-up testing if you have no symptoms of hyperglycemia.

mainEntity.name: How do I confirm if my 16mmol glucose reading is accurate?

acceptedAnswer.text: First, wash and fully dry your hands, then retest with a new unexpired test strip following manufacturer instructions. If you get a similar result, run a control solution test to confirm your meter is working correctly. If results are still high, follow your care team’s hyperglycemia protocol.

mainEntity.name: Is 16mmol/L a dangerous blood sugar level for people with diabetes?

acceptedAnswer.text: For people with Type 1 diabetes, 16mmol/L carries a significant risk of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and requires immediate ketone testing and possible insulin adjustment. For Type 2 diabetes or prediabetes, it is a sign of uncontrolled hyperglycemia that needs prompt follow-up, though immediate risk is lower unless you have symptoms like confusion or persistent nausea.

mainEntity.name: What should I do first after getting a 16mmol/L reading?

acceptedAnswer.text: First, rule out testing errors by washing your hands, using a new test strip, and retesting. If the reading is confirmed, check for symptoms of hyperglycemia like frequent thirst, fatigue, or blurred vision, then follow your personalized care plan for high blood sugar.

mainEntity.name: Can dehydration cause a false 16mmol/L blood sugar reading?

acceptedAnswer.text: Severe dehydration can both cause actual high blood sugar and skew home glucose test results, leading to artificially elevated readings. If you are dehydrated, rehydrate with plain water and retest 30 minutes later to confirm your reading.
